Complicit

/kuhm-PLIS-it/ - the stress falls on PLIS · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Complicit means involved as a knowing partner in wrongdoing.

The timekeeper who logged twelve-hour shifts as eight was complicit in the mill's scheme to cheat its weavers of overtime.

Worked Example

The diamond appraiser insisted he had merely valued the stones brought to him; but he had valued the same stolen stones five times under five different names, and the court held him complicit in the fencing ring.

Complicit is precise about two things at once: participation and knowledge. A courier who unknowingly carries stolen goods is involved but not complicit — the word requires that you understood the wrong and lent yourself to it anyway.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

involved: caught up in it, perhaps innocently; complicit adds knowledge

cooperating: working together — with no shade of crime over it

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

innocent: having no part in the wrong

unwitting: unaware of what was afoot — the opposite of knowing

Where it sits · how much guilt one shares — unaware → aware → complicit

unaware vs. complicit: Someone wholly unaware of a scheme cannot share its guilt; unaware sits at the bottom of the ladder and stops far short of complicit.

aware vs. complicit: To be aware of wrongdoing and stay silent is troubling, but aware stops short of complicit, which requires playing a knowing part.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — com-

Prefix — com-: together

Root — plic

Root — plic: to fold

Suffix — -it

Suffix — -it: adjective ending

Put it together

Put it together: Com- (together) + plic (to fold) + -it = folded together. Latin plicare, 'to fold,' runs all through English — a complicated case has its threads folded over one another — and the complicit partner is folded into the crime itself, wrapped inside its plan.

Use the root in a new word: complicated

Use the root in a new word: complicated: A complicated knot is exactly what it says — strands folded together until they are hard to trace.

Word Choice

formal

Complicit describes what you are; abet (also in this unit) names what you do. A silent witness is sometimes called complicit in a loose, accusing way, but strictly the word wants both knowledge and a part played — save it for the partner, not the bystander.
